clue.text: Generous applause? Not much

parts.note: to give someone a hand is to applaud them
some means a modest amount, not a lot

explanation.surface: A grudging audience offers only a smattering of clapping.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark invites reading 'Generous applause' as one idea, but 'Generous' stands alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A handsome sum or gift is a liberal, ample one, so the word is a synonym for open-handed.

clue.text: Flexible chair duly moved under pressure

indicators.note: something flexible bends and changes shape, so these letters are bent into a new order

explanation.surface: An adjustable office chair is moved about under strain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flexible' signals rearranging CHAIR and DULY together.
explanation.definitionFit: Hydraulic machinery is driven by liquid forced through pipes at high pressure.

clue.text: Sense I'm out for revenge

indicators.note: out here means put out of order, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone senses they are being sought for vengeance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' signals an anagram of SENSE plus IM; the apostrophe adds no letter.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the goddess of retribution gave her name to any deserved downfall or vengeance.

clue.text: Patch of nettles is near

explanation.surface: A clump of stinging weeds lies close by.
explanation.walkthrough: Here 'near' is the British sense of tight-fisted; the first reading is the rarer adjective meaning full of stings, said with a hard g.
explanation.definitionFit: A bed of nettles is full of stings, while a near person is mean with money, a miser.

clue.text: Crime fiction in which priests classically played leading role

definitions.text: in which priests classically played leading role

explanation.surface: A detective story where clergymen take the lead.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is the secret religious rites of ancient Greece, such as those at Eleusis, led by priests.
explanation.definitionFit: Whodunits are a genre of novels, and the ancient secret cults of initiation were sacred rites run by priests.

clue.text: Ambassador meeting island's tragic queen

parts.note: an ambassador is addressed as His Excellency, abbreviated HE
Cuba is a Caribbean island; the possessive adds no letter

explanation.surface: A diplomat visits a Caribbean island.
explanation.definitionFit: She was Priam's wife, Queen of Troy, whose sorrows feature in Euripides' tragedy.

clue.text: Artist's house and garden

parts.note: a garth is an old or northern word for an enclosed yard or garden

explanation.surface: A painter's home and its grounds.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's reads as 'is': the artist is house plus garden.
explanation.definitionFit: William Hogarth was the eighteenth-century English painter and engraver of satirical series.

clue.text: Lake gave delight to Mellors

explanation.surface: A lake's beauty enchanted a gamekeeper.
explanation.walkthrough: Lake Constance lies between Germany, Austria and Switzerland; Mellors is the gamekeeper lover of Lady Chatterley in D H Lawrence's novel, and her first name fits.
explanation.definitionFit: The large Alpine lake on the Rhine bears this name, as does Lady Chatterley, the gamekeeper's lover.

clue.text: An evergreen, yet bare, strangely

indicators.note: strangely suggests things put in an odd order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Oddly, a tree that keeps its leaves looks leafless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strangely' signals an anagram of YET and BARE.
explanation.definitionFit: Laurel, the sweet bay, keeps its leaves all year and is grown as a clipped shrub.

clue.text: Centre-back is dark

indicators.note: back tells us to read the word for centre from end to start

parts.note: mid means middle or centre

explanation.surface: A football defender in the middle is a bit dim-witted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Centre-back' looks like the football position; split it, 'back' reverses MID.
explanation.definitionFit: A dim room is gloomy, lacking light.

clue.text: Rising inches — need for immediate action

parts.note: INS is the abbreviation for inches
urgency is pressing need demanding prompt action

explanation.surface: Something climbs slowly while a crisis demands action.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rising' is the noun, an uprising, not the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A rising is a revolt, and a rebellion against authority is a synonym.

clue.text: Told off because design is faulty

parts.note: as can mean because, as in 'as it was late'

indicators.note: faulty here means wrongly put together, so the letters are reordered

explanation.surface: Someone is scolded because their design has a flaw.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Told off' here means detailed for a duty, as soldiers are told off for guard, not scolded; 'faulty' signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: To be told off for a task is to be allotted or detailed to it.

clue.text: Vessel's swift return

explanation.surface: A ship makes a quick trip home.
explanation.walkthrough: The vessel is a laboratory flask with a bent neck, not a ship; the return is a quick reply.
explanation.definitionFit: A chemist's distilling flask has this name, as does a sharp, witty reply.

clue.text: Not having known where one is, see the way

definitions.text: Not having known where one is

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning look or see
ST is the abbreviation for street, a way

explanation.surface: A bewildered traveller is told to look at the road.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone without bearings, unsure of their whereabouts, is astray.

clue.text: Clocks fast runner for the flat, perhaps

parts.note: to clock a runner is to time them, so clocks means times
the hare is the proverbial swift runner

explanation.surface: At the races, someone times a speedy runner on the Flat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the flat' suggests flat racing, the British horse racing on level courses, but it is an apartment owned in shares.
explanation.definitionFit: A holiday apartment owned jointly, each owner using it for set weeks, is an example.

clue.text: Arrogant, like one attempting a slam-dunk?

explanation.surface: A cocky basketball player goes for a showy dunk.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading is literal: a player slam-dunking reaches up with hands raised high.
explanation.definitionFit: Overbearing behaviour is domineering, and a dunker's hands are lifted above the rim.

clue.text: Crab seen at extremities of bay

explanation.surface: A crustacean is spotted at either end of a bay.
explanation.walkthrough: The bay is a reddish-brown horse, not a coast, and its extremities are its hooves, where the iron shoes go.
explanation.definitionFit: The king crab is named for its curved shell, and a farrier nails such iron to a horse's hooves.

clue.text: Holy orders stonily received in desert once

definitions.text: Holy orders stonily received in desert once

parts.words: Holy orders stonily received in desert once
parts.note: the holy orders are divine commands, not ordination; they were received on tablets of stone by Moses in the Sinai wilderness

explanation.surface: Priests were once ordained coldly in the wilderness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Holy orders' suggests ordination to the priesthood; read literally it means sacred commands, carved on stone at Sinai.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ten Commandments were given to Moses on two stone tablets on Mount Sinai.

clue.text: Joint available from chef, no problem

parts.note: a commis is a junior chef in a professional kitchen
sure is a casual way of saying certainly, no problem

explanation.surface: A butcher's cut of meat can be had from the cook without fuss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joint' suggests a cut of meat from the chef; it is an anatomical seam or junction.
explanation.definitionFit: In anatomy this is a junction or seam where two parts meet, such as nerve fibres crossing.

clue.text: Go past old battle site where duke became king

indicators.note: became says one letter is replaced by another, duke turning into king

parts.note: Verdun in France was the site of a great First World War battle
R, for rex, is the abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: Travelling past a historic battlefield where a duke was crowned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'where duke became king' signals the swap; R stands for rex, Latin for king. Verdun's First World War battle makes it the 'old battle site'.
explanation.definitionFit: To overshoot a mark or limit is to run beyond it.

clue.text: Tree Wallace set by West African river

definitions.text: Wallace set by West African river

explanation.surface: A tree grows beside an African river in an adventure story.
explanation.walkthrough: Edgar Wallace wrote 'Sanders of the River', about a colonial commissioner in Nigeria; the tree is red sandalwood.
explanation.definitionFit: Red sandalwood is a timber tree with this name, which is also Edgar Wallace's commissioner hero.

clue.text: End of the film, a long one

indicators.note: end of tells us to take the final letter of the next word

parts.note: a pic is an informal word for a film or picture

explanation.surface: The closing scene of a lengthy movie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a long one' means a long film, picking up 'film' from the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A blockbuster spanning great events and running for hours is a grand-scale picture.

clue.text: Runs into mischievous child to make sharp point

indicators.note: into says one piece goes inside another

parts.note: a pickle is a playful word for a naughty child
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A naughty child runs about, needling someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'into' puts R, the cricket abbreviation for runs, inside PICKLE.
explanation.definitionFit: A thorn or spine on a plant is a small sharp point.

clue.text: Anger as painting supplies fall short

indicators.note: fall short means the word stops one letter before its end

parts.note: tempera is a paint made with egg yolk, an artist's material

explanation.surface: An artist is furious when their paints run out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fall short' drops the last letter of TEMPERA.
explanation.definitionFit: Losing one's temper means flying into a rage, so the word means a fit of fury.

clue.text: Each boy's present appearing in this

parts.note: per means for each, as in 'a pound per head'
a son is a boy; the possessive adds no letter

explanation.surface: Every lad's gift shows up somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is cryptic: someone present and appearing in the flesh is said to come 'in person'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being physically there, rather than by letter or deputy, is the idiom 'in person'.

clue.text: About average for slow learners

parts.note: re means about or concerning
medial can mean average or middle

explanation.surface: A discussion of typical marks in a special-needs class.
explanation.definitionFit: Remedial classes give extra help to pupils who struggle.

clue.text: All who see papers for university post

explanation.surface: Newspaper readers are offered a university job.
explanation.walkthrough: In British universities a reader is a senior academic rank just below professor.
explanation.definitionFit: A paper's audience is its total of readers, and the post of reader is a senior lectureship.

clue.text: Sort of beer finally drunk as example

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of the word drunk

parts.note: EG is the abbreviation for 'for example'

explanation.surface: A drinker downs a sample of beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finally' takes K from 'drunk'.
explanation.definitionFit: Keg beer is filtered, pasteurised and served under gas pressure from a metal cask.

clue.text: In conjunction, dare one say "more"?

parts.note: a joining word in grammar which, split as a prefix meaning not plus a word for fewer, jokingly means 'not fewer', that is more

explanation.surface: Someone at a joint event hesitates to ask for extra.
explanation.walkthrough: 'conjunction' is grammatical, a joining word like 'if'; split into UN- and LESS, it reads as 'not less'.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a conjunction meaning 'except if', and split up it facetiously means not fewer.

clue.text: On people acting together, old magistrate pronounced reduced sentence

indicators.note: in an across clue, one thing on another means it follows it

parts.note: a rep is a repertory company, actors performing together

indicators.note: pronounced says the word is to be taken by its sound

parts.note: a reeve was a local magistrate or official in medieval England

explanation.surface: An ancient judge, speaking on behalf of a theatre troupe, lightens a punishment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' places the magistrate after the actors, as is usual in across clues; 'pronounced' means only the sound of the old title counts, not its spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: A stay of execution commutes or postpones a punishment, often a death penalty.
